html:
Nan Madol is a ruined city built on nearly a hundred small artificial islands in a lagoon off the island of Pohnpei in Micronesia. It was the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled all of Pohnpei, until about 1628.

The islets were built of long, natural columns of black basalt, stacked crosswise like logs, with coral rubble filling the inside. Some walls rise several metres, and some stones weigh tons; how they were moved is still not fully known. Canals run between the islets, which is why it is sometimes called the Venice of the Pacific. The site had two parts: one for the rulers and their priests, and one, Nan Douwas, for royal burials.

Building of the megalithic walls began around 1180 to 1200. Oral tradition says Saudeleur rule became harsh and was overthrown by Isokelekel, a hero from another island, who set up the chiefly system that still exists on Pohnpei. Nan Madol was then slowly abandoned. It was listed as World Heritage in 2016. It is one of the great stone works of the Pacific, with the moai of Rapa Nui.
